title: The services page an independent hotel actually needs
metaTitle: Services page an independent hotel needs
excerpt: List the stay in a guest's words. Each item needs an outcome, a boundary, and a way to check dates. A grid of vague capabilities does not help.
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases, a specific room rather than a list of vague comforts.
caption: The sofa, the windows, and the vases are nameable objects. Hotel services should be too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a hotel services page list?
faqs.answer: The parts of the stay a guest asks about: the room, breakfast, arrival, and parking or the lack of it. Write each one as an outcome, a boundary, and a link to check dates. Department names such as guest relations are less clear than the desk.

faqs.question: How specific should a boundary be?
faqs.answer: Specific enough to prevent a bad booking: breakfast ends at a named hour, dogs are welcome in one room only, and stairs are stated if there is no elevator. Soft lines about a restful atmosphere do not do this job.

faqs.question: Why avoid an icon grid?
faqs.answer: Icons labeled comfort or design fit every hotel with a website. They cannot carry a boundary, such as which room allows a dog. Keep a paragraph a night manager could say. Cut any cell you could not point to on a tour.

markdown:
An independent hotel services page should list the stay in the words a traveler already uses. For someone comparing three properties, each item needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, which is to check dates. A grid of vague capabilities does not help them choose.

Google's people-first guidance is a useful test. After reading, a person should feel they learned enough to do the thing they came to do. On this page the thing is to understand what the stay contains, where it stops, and how to see if their nights are free. A tile that says "experiences" leaves them needing another search, which is the failure that guidance warns against.

## Name the stay, not the department

Travelers do not shop for departments. They shop for a bed, a morning, a way to arrive, and a person to ask. Write those. "Front office," "guest relations," and "food and beverage" are how a large hotel organizes staff. An independent house can say "the desk," "breakfast," and "the room" and be clearer.

Use the words they type and the words they say on the phone. Rooms. Breakfast. Arrival. Parking. Dogs. Quiet hours. If your regulars say "the courtyard room" and "the small double," use those names. A renamed "deluxe sanctuary" forces them to translate, and translation is where doubt starts.

Four to seven items is a full page. More than that and you are listing chores. Fewer than that and you may be hiding the thing that decides the stay, often parking or stairs. Count the questions the desk answers every week. Those questions are the outline. Marketing categories are not.

Put the room first if the homepage has not already done the full job, or put breakfast first if that is why people pick you over the other two. Order is an argument. Lead with the item that changes the comparison, then the item people worry about, then the rest.

## Outcome in the guest's words

Each item should say what the guest gets, in one or two sentences, with a concrete noun. Breakfast: a seat, an hour, a kind of food. The desk: a person present from this time until that time, and what they can actually do, such as call a cab or hold a bag. The room: the bed, the window, the bath, repeated only if this page is where the detail lives. Do not paste the homepage and call it a service.

Outcome is not a promise of transformation. "You will feel restored" is a mood. "You can work at the desk under the window if you need an hour between meetings" is an outcome, and it has a boundary hiding inside it: one desk, one hour, not a conference room. Specific is kinder, because it lets the wrong guest opt out.

Write the sentence the way the night manager would say it. Short. A little plain. If a sentence needs the word "curated," it is not finished. Replace the adjective with the object. A bowl of fruit is an object. A philosophy of welcome is not.

If an item varies by room, say which room. A bathtub in one room and a shower in the others is two outcomes. Listing "luxury bathing" as a single service is how the shower guest ends up disappointed and precise about it in public.

## The boundary

A boundary is the edge of the offer. It belongs in the same block as the outcome, not in a policy PDF. Breakfast ends at 10. The desk is not staffed from midnight to seven, and here is the number that still works. Dogs are welcome in the courtyard room, not on the beds, and not in the breakfast room. Children are welcome, or the house is adults only, with the age written as a number.

Boundaries are not a lack of hospitality. They are how a small building stays pleasant for the people already in it. A traveler comparing three stays is often trying to avoid a mismatch: a celebration that needs a bar you do not have, a wheelchair that your stairs cannot take, a remote worker who needs silence you cannot offer because the street is lively until eleven.

Say the stair count if there is no elevator. Say that the walls are old if the walls are old. A romantic adjective will not soundproof a room. The guest who needs quiet will thank you for the sentence and book somewhere else. The guest who likes a lively street will book you. Both outcomes are success for the page.

Do not soften a boundary into a riddle. "We encourage a restful atmosphere" is not a quiet hour. "Quiet from 9 p.m. in the rooms" is a boundary. House rules can be warm and still be rules. Warmth is the tone. The hour is the content.

## One next step

Each block ends the same way: check dates. The link can be smarter than a generic button. Breakfast's block can pass the guest toward the checker with a note that breakfast is in the rate, or not. The dog block can remind them to mention the dog in the request if your checker cannot hold that fact. The stairs block can point at the room that starts on the ground floor, if you have one.

Do not end a block with "learn more" unless there is a real page behind it. "Learn more" stacked six times is how a services page becomes a corridor. If the detail fits in the block, keep it there. This page is allowed to be the destination.

One action is enough. A second action, "join the list," splits the decision. The traveler comparing three stays did not come to subscribe. They came to see if Tuesday is free and whether the dog can come. Serve that. The list can live in the footer for people who are not ready.

If a service requires a human, such as a buyout of all the rooms, say so, and say what to have ready: dates, the number of rooms, the reason. That path is the exception. Label it as the exception so ordinary nights stay on the checker.

## Four items, written as decisions

A useful services page for a small hotel often comes down to four blocks. You may have a fifth. You rarely need a twelfth.

The room. Outcome: a night in this specific room, described as it is. Boundary: occupancy, size in honest language, the window, the bath. Next step: check dates for this room, not for "a room."

Breakfast. Outcome: what is served, where, and the last sitting. Boundary: what a special diet needs in notice, and whether children eat the same meal. Next step: check dates, with breakfast named as included or as a price.

Arrival. Outcome: the earliest and latest you can realistically receive someone, and where they should stand if they are early. Boundary: no luggage room, or a luggage room the size of a closet. Next step: check dates, then write only if the arrival is outside those hours.

The street and the car. Outcome: how to arrive on foot or by train, in minutes. Boundary: parking is two spaces, or there is no parking, and a garage three minutes away charges its own fee. Next step: check dates if the access still works for them.

Read the four blocks to someone who has stayed with you. Ask which sentence is too flattering. Believe them. Guests are better editors of services pages than brand decks are, because they remember the stair and forget the adjective.

## What a capability grid does instead

A grid of six icons with two-word labels feels like a website. It is a contents page with the contents removed. "Comfort." "Design." "Local." The traveler cannot tell whether comfort means a good mattress or a robe. They cannot tell whether local means a map or a person who will walk them to dinner.

Icons do not carry the boundary. A small pictogram of a dog does not say "courtyard room only." The sentence does. If you love the icon, keep it as a marker beside a real paragraph. Do not let it replace the paragraph.

Capabilities also drift into the hotel's hopes. "Bespoke celebrations" on a property with one table for sixteen is a boundary problem disguised as a service. Either describe the table, the curfew, and the fact that you do not have a planner on staff, or remove the tile. Hope is not a service.

Look at the grid and ask, for each cell, what the guest holds in their hand at the end. A key, a plate, a parking instruction, a no. If you cannot name the object, cut the cell.

## After the stay is itemized

Someone who believes the items still wants to know who stands behind them at eleven at night. That is the about page, and it should name a person, not a legend. [Who is actually on the property](/blog/how-an-independent-hotel-should-write-an-about-page) is the right next read, because a list of services without a responsible human is still a brochure.

For a sense of how a studio builds pages around a real offer, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The standard is the same as the desk standard: say what the thing is, where it stops, and what the person can do next.
